It can depend on the numbers in question. A few ideas:

  1. The way a ALU does it
    Numbers such as 17 are good for this, specifically due to being mostly 0s when written in binary (10001 here).
    The point is to see it as 13x(16 + 1), where 16 is a power of 2.
    This means you can do it by putting one lot of 13 aside, then doubling the 13 four times (26, 52, 104, 208). Optionally, you can imagine the 16 halving down to 1 when you do it (8, 4, 2, 1).
    Your 13x(16 + 1) is now 208 + 13, or 221.

  2. Memorize square numbers and only multiply to get the remainder
    A good tradeoff with doing this is no longer having to remember shit such as 11x12 (i.e. just do 122 - 12).
    If you can commit to memory 132 = 169 and/or 172 = 289 then you can think of it as 13x(13 + 4) or 17*(17 - 4).
    Taking the former, do 13x4 normally to get 52, and add it to 132 = 169 to get 169 + 52 = 221

  3. Memorize fewer square numbers and use Difference Of Two Squares (DOTS) In this case, 152 = 225 is the useful quantity.
    Thinking of 13x17 as (15 - 2)(15 + 2), DOTS tells us that this equals 152 - 22 = 225 - 4 = 221.

Sometimes there will be tricks possible which rely on counting base 10 and such, but the more general idea above is to change the expression into something with more steps but easier to do. Keep yourself free to choose how you distribute that, e.g. if (10 + 3)(20 - 3) = 200 + 30 - 9 works for you then do that instead.
